mcq.q: A rollback restored the code but not the prompt and index. The missing practice is…
options: Feature flags for each prompt, index and model change
A release manifest versioning everything that changes behaviour
More tests before each release goes out to production
Faster CI so that rollbacks finish in a few minutes
mcq.why: Behaviour depends on code, prompts, models, indexes and config together.
distractors: Flags switch versions; they do not record the whole set.
Tests do not restore the old prompt and index.
Speed does not fix a partial rollback.

mcq.q: What is a release manifest?
options: A marketing note announcing the release
A list of the servers the release runs on
A changelog that covers the code only
One ID bundling versions of all that changes behaviour
mcq.why: Code, prompts, tools, model, embedder, index, config and evaluation suite.
distractors: Prompts, models and indexes change behaviour too.

mcq.q: Only the prompt changes. Does the release ID change?
options: Yes: any behaviour-changing input means a new ID
Only for major changes to the prompt
No, since none of the code changed
Only if some of the tests then fail
mcq.why: Prompts change behaviour.
distractors: The ID tracks change, not test results.

mcq.q: Why should traces carry the release ID?
options: To reproduce outputs and bisect regressions
To save tokens on later calls
Because OTel requires a release ID
For billing each customer correctly
mcq.why: Links outputs to the exact system.

mcq.q: An auditor asks the team to reproduce an answer from last month exactly. Which artefacts must the release manifest have versioned? Choose all that apply.
options: Model and embedder revisions, and the index
Prompts and tool schemas
The office Wi-Fi password
The evaluation suite
mcq.why: Everything that can change behaviour.

mcq.q: A rollback restored the code but left a new prompt and index live. What happens?
options: Everything is restored to the old state
The new prompt is ignored by the old code
The mismatched combination may keep failing
The index rolls itself back automatically
mcq.why: Roll back the whole manifest.
distractors: Indexes do not roll back on their own.

mcq.q: Why version the evaluation suite in the manifest?
options: Suites never change once they are written
Results compare only when you know which suite ran
For licence tracking of the suite's test data
To make each release larger and more complete
mcq.why: Suites grow over time (17.9).

mcq.q: Should an ACL or permissions watermark be part of the manifest, as in Harbor's?
options: Only for code, not data state
Only in staging, not production
Never; permissions are not versioned
Yes, if it changes which documents are used
mcq.why: Anything that changes behaviour belongs there.
distractors: Data state can change behaviour too.
Production behaviour depends on it most.
They affect which documents are used.

mcq.q: What makes a manifest useful for audits?
options: It is deleted after each release goes out to save space
It is immutable and kept with traces for the retention period
It can be edited after the release whenever it is needed
It lives in a chat message to the team, pinned to the channel
mcq.why: Auditors need to reconstruct the system.

mcq.q: Two releases differ only in index version. What can bisecting show?
options: The model's weights at the time
Network latency between regions
Whether the index change caused it
Nothing useful about the change
mcq.why: Manifests let you isolate a single changed input.

mcq.q: At 2 a.m. a release that changed the prompt, the index and some code shows a regression, and the cause is unclear. What should on-call roll back?
options: The whole previous release manifest
The prompt only, as the likeliest cause
Whatever changed last in the release
The code only, as it is easiest to revert
mcq.why: Restore a coherent, compatible system.
distractors: Order does not identify the cause.

mcq.q: A team changes retrieval k from 8 to 20 in a config file without producing a new release ID. A regression appears, but bisecting by release shows no change. What went wrong?
options: Config that changes behaviour must be in the manifest, giving a new release ID
Bisecting only works for code changes, so it was the wrong tool
k cannot change behaviour, so the regression lies elsewhere
The traces should have stored the full prompt instead of the ID
mcq.why: Any behaviour-affecting input belongs in the manifest; otherwise bisecting cannot find it.
distractors: Bisecting works on any versioned input.
More passages change answers, cost and latency.
The release ID is what links outputs to versions.

mcq.q: Shadow deployments must never…
options: Read data from production stores
Call tools that write
Use copies of real user traffic
Log traces for later comparison
mcq.why: Shadowing a write creates real duplicate actions.
distractors: Read-only access is how shadowing works.
Shadowing uses copies of real traffic.
Shadow runs should be traced to compare results.

mcq.q: What is a shadow deployment?
options: A backup region kept warm so traffic can fail over during an outage
A hidden feature behind a flag that only internal staff can switch on
A canary that takes half of the live traffic and shows its answers to users
Copies of real requests go to the new version; its outputs are compared, never shown
mcq.why: No user risk.

mcq.q: A team wants to expose a new prompt to real users with little risk, comparing it against the baseline before going wider. Roughly what share of traffic should that first step get?
mcq.why: Compare with the baseline in the same window.

mcq.q: Does rollback undo actions the bad version took?
options: No: past actions stay done; plan reconciliation
Only refunds, which the system can reverse
Only messages, which the system can recall
Yes, always: rollback undoes every action
mcq.why: Compensation needs its own plan.
distractors: Rollback changes versions, not past actions.

mcq.q: What must rollback be?
options: One fast action, with the old version still deployed and compatible
A weekend project for the platform team to plan and carry out
A full rebuild of every component from the previous commit
Optional, as long as the canary looked healthy before promotion
mcq.why: Practise it.

mcq.q: In the gate-driven rollout figure, what happens if “rollback rehearsed” is unticked?
options: Promotion is refused
Nothing changes in the rollout
The rollout continues as before
It jumps straight to 100%
mcq.why: Every gate must be ticked to advance.

mcq.q: A controlled rollout by cohort usually starts with…
options: Random external users, chosen evenly
Internal users, then low-risk tenants
The largest customers, for most signal
All users at once, for a fast result
mcq.why: Exposure increases in steps.

mcq.q: What happens in automated canary analysis when a metric breaches its bound?
options: Traffic doubles to collect more data
An email is sent, and nothing else
The baseline is changed to match
Traffic goes back to 0% and the release fails
mcq.why: Automatic rollback.

mcq.q: How should agents be shadowed?
options: With the real write tools enabled, for realism
Not at all; agents can never be shadowed
Only with mocked tools that have no side effects
Only at night, when traffic and risk are low
mcq.why: Shadow traffic must never reach write tools.
distractors: Timing does not remove side effects.

mcq.q: A release swaps the retrieval index for one built with a new embedding model. What must be true for its rollback to be safe?
options: Nothing
Deleting the old index
Keeping the old index warm (10.7)
Rebuilding the old index on rollback
mcq.why: Rebuilding takes hours.

mcq.q: A canary takes 5% of 40,000 requests an hour for 2 hours, and a judge scores a 10% sample of the canary's answers. How many answers are judged?
mcq.why: 40,000 × 0.05 × 2 = 4,000 canary requests; 10% of them is 400.
distractors: That is all the canary's requests.

mcq.q: A bad prompt sent wrong refund confirmations to 300 customers before it was rolled back. What does the chapter say happens next?
options: Nothing more, because the rollback reverted the messages already sent
Wait for the customers to complain, then deal with each case as it comes
Rollback does not undo those messages: find the customers, reconcile and communicate
Roll back a second time so that the wrong confirmations are recalled
mcq.why: Past actions stay done; plan reconciliation or compensation.
distractors: Rolling back changes versions, not past actions.

mcq.q: A candidate improves average accuracy but fails one cross-tenant case. Decision?
options: Ship, as the average improved
Block release
Ship to half of the tenants
Ignore one case out of many
mcq.why: Critical invariants block regardless of average improvements.
distractors: The leak could hit any tenant.

mcq.q: What is a release gate?
options: A feature flag that turns each release on or off
A firewall rule in front of the production API
An automated check that blocks promotion below a threshold
A manual approval email sent to the release owner
mcq.why: Gates enforce acceptance and release criteria.
distractors: Network control, not a release check.

mcq.q: Choose all four gates in the chapter.
options: Quality
Design review of colours
Safety / security
Performance and cost
mcq.why: Quality, safety/security, performance and cost.

mcq.q: Why are all four gates needed?
options: Different changes fail different gates
Regulations require exactly four
One gate is enough on its own
To slow releases down on purpose
mcq.why: e.g. a cheaper model fails quality; a new tool fails security.

mcq.q: A quality threshold says “overall ≥ baseline − 0.5 points (within CI); no language drops > 2 points”. A candidate is +1 overall but −3 in one language. Does it pass?
options: No: the language gate fails
Yes, since it is within the CI
Yes, since overall accuracy improved
It cannot be told from these numbers
mcq.why: Per-segment gates block hidden regressions.

mcq.q: Cost gate: cost per successful task ≤ +10% unless approved. Current $0.050; candidate $0.057. What happens?
options: Blocked: any rise in cost fails
Blocked unless approved: +14%
Passes: the rise is about +7%
Passes: it is still under $0.06
distractors: The gate is relative, not an absolute $0.06.

mcq.q: Is a green CI badge proof that every production failure is covered?
options: Only for the security checks, not others
No: gates cover only what is in the suites
Yes, as long as every gate shows green
Only for the quality checks, not others
mcq.why: Keep adding production failures (17.9).
distractors: Coverage is limited for every gate.
Coverage is limited for every gate.

mcq.q: Which threshold belongs to the safety/security gate?
options: Cost ≤ +10%
Overall quality ≥ baseline
0 cross-tenant leaks
p95 TTFT ≤ 1.5 s
mcq.why: Plus injection success ≤ baseline and no critical CVEs.

mcq.q: What does the laptop lab's gate.py do?
options: Deploys the build to production once the tests have finished running
Computes overall and critical pass rates; exits non-zero below thresholds
Writes the release notes from the results of the evaluation run
Trains a new model on the failing cases so that the next run passes
mcq.why: A non-zero exit fails the CI job.

mcq.q: Why should judge-based quality metrics include confidence intervals?
options: Judges are always wrong
To slow the gate down
To look more scientific
Small differences may be noise
mcq.why: Compare within CI.

mcq.q: The cost gate allows cost per successful task to rise by up to 10% without approval. The current release costs $0.040 per success, the candidate $0.043. What happens?
options: It passes only because the amounts are under $0.05
Blocked: the rise is 30%, far over the gate
It passes: a 7.5% rise is within the 10% gate
Blocked: any rise in cost needs approval
distractors: 3 tenths of a cent on 4 cents is 7.5%.

mcq.q: Switching to a cheaper model passes the quality and cost gates, but in the load test p99 total time rises to 15 s against a 12 s threshold. What happens?
options: The latency threshold is raised to 15 s for this release
It ships, since p95 is what matters to users
The performance gate blocks promotion until latency is fixed
It ships, since quality and cost both passed
mcq.why: Each gate must pass; different changes fail different gates.
distractors: Moving the gate hides the regression.
The threshold is set on p99.

mcq.q: What does “build once, promote the same artefact” prevent?
options: Rollbacks to earlier releases
Shipping something never tested
Fast deploys to production
Using a staging environment
mcq.why: Rebuilding per environment means you never tested what you shipped.

mcq.q: What should differ between staging and production?
options: The prompts used in each environment
The model version each environment calls
Only configuration such as credentials and capacity
The container image digest that is deployed
mcq.why: Same artefacts, different config.

mcq.q: What is GitOps?
options: A CI vendor's hosted service for building images
Using Git to store the application code only
Desired state in a repo; a controller syncs clusters to it
Manual console changes, logged in a shared sheet
mcq.why: Gives an audit trail and rollback by revert.

mcq.q: A container downloads “latest” model weights at start-up. What is the problem?
options: Downloads at start-up make the containers slow to become ready
It saves storage in the image, which is good practice anyway
Nothing; the latest weights are always the best ones to run
Not reproducible: staging and production may run different models
mcq.why: Pin model revisions.

mcq.q: Choose all the infrastructure the chapter says should be defined in code.
options: Dashboards and alerts
Queues, gateways and IAM
GPU node pools and vector databases
Engineers' calendars
mcq.why: Reviewed and applied by pipelines.

mcq.q: Which pins a base image most precisely?
options: Its size
Its tag
Its name
Its digest
mcq.why: Tags can move.

mcq.q: Why should staging mirror production's shape?
options: It does not matter for tests, only for demos
So tests mean something: same engine, index, data
To cost the same as production each month
For marketing screenshots of the product
mcq.why: Different shapes give misleading results.

mcq.q: Which tools are named for infrastructure as code?
options: Jaeger, Grafana Loki and Prometheus
OpenTofu/Terraform, Pulumi, Helm/Kustomize
k6, Locust, JMeter and Gatling tools
garak, PyRIT and promptfoo red-team
mcq.why: Observability, red teaming and load testing are other chapters.

mcq.q: A hotfix is applied directly in production, and the next GitOps sync removes it. What should have happened?
options: Nothing; GitOps was right to remove the change
It should go through the repo, so the state includes it
Apply the fix twice so that it sticks this time
Disable GitOps for that service from now on
mcq.why: The repository is the source of truth.

mcq.q: Which stage runs full gates (evaluation, security, load, cost)?
options: Dev
The developer laptop only
None
Staging
mcq.why: Dev runs smoke tests; staging runs full gates.

mcq.q: Staging rebuilt the image from a commit and passed every gate. Production rebuilt it again from the same commit, pulled a new base layer, and failed. What practice was missing?
options: A longer canary in production to catch the failure sooner
More tests in production after every deploy finishes
Build once and promote the same image digest, with base images pinned
Deploying from developers' laptops instead of from CI
mcq.why: Rebuilding per environment means you never tested what you shipped.
distractors: It would only catch the failure later.
The problem is that a different artefact shipped.

mcq.q: Staging runs a small CPU engine with a flat vector index, while production uses vLLM and HNSW. Staging load tests pass, but production misses its latency SLO. What does the chapter recommend?
options: Make staging mirror production's shape: same engine, index type, realistic data
Use the same small CPU engine in production as well, so they match
Load-test in production only from now on, skipping staging entirely
Raise the production latency SLO so that it matches what staging shows
mcq.why: Tests mean something only on a production-like environment.
distractors: That changes production, not the test.
Staging exists to catch problems first.

mcq.q: Why treat a model upgrade as a release?
options: Providers require it in their terms of service
It is faster than doing a normal library upgrade
Behaviour changes hit prompts, formats, cost and refusals
Models never change between versions in practice
mcq.why: Run the full suite.

mcq.q: In the compatibility report, current prompts on the new model lose 1.8 points with 9 critical regressions. What is the action?
options: Lower the gate
Drop the model forever
Ship
Re-tune the prompt
mcq.why: The re-tuned prompt then gained 2.4 points with 0 critical regressions.

mcq.q: Median output tokens rose 38%. What does it affect?
options: Nothing
Cost and latency
Only tokenisation
Only quality
mcq.why: Add length guidance and re-check the cost gate.

mcq.q: Output tokens are 70% of cost per task and rise 38%. About how much does cost per task rise?
options: About 70%
About 38%
About 10%
About 27%
distractors: That assumes all cost is output.

mcq.q: Choose all the checks the chapter lists for a model upgrade.
options: The provider's logo
Tokenizer differences and supported parameters
Structured-output adherence and tool-call format
Refusal behaviour and verbosity
mcq.why: Run with current and re-tuned prompts.

mcq.q: A team calls a “latest” alias and the provider moves it. What protects them?
options: Nothing; aliases are safe to rely on
Pinned snapshots plus scheduled re-evaluation
A different SDK for calling the provider
A larger request timeout on every call
mcq.why: Aliases can change silently.
distractors: The SDK does not pin models.

mcq.q: Embedding model change: how must queries and documents switch?
options: Atomically, with blue/green indexes
Documents first, queries next month
It does not matter
Queries first, documents later
mcq.why: Mixed embedding spaces do not match (10.7).

mcq.q: A fine-tuned model's base gets a new version. What is needed?
options: Only re-tokenising the data
Nothing; adapters carry over
Only a quick smoke test
Re-run fine-tuning and 13.6's checks
mcq.why: Adapters depend on the exact base.
distractors: They are tied to the base.

mcq.q: Over-refusal on the should-answer set rose from 1.2% to 3.1%. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, since it is within normal noise
Investigate the categories; adjust the system prompt
Raise the temperature to vary the answers
Ship it, since refusing is always the safe choice
mcq.why: Over-refusal blocks legitimate users.

mcq.q: JSON schema adherence without constrained decoding fell from 99.8% to 99.1% on the new model. What is the report's action?
options: Enable constrained decoding
Raise the temperature
Drop JSON output entirely
Ship it as it is
mcq.why: Constrained decoding enforces the schema (7.4).

mcq.q: A new model's median output length is 38% higher. Output tokens are 60% of the cost per task. Roughly how much does the cost per task rise, and what does the 10% cost gate say?
options: About 38%, the same as the change in output length
About 23%, so the cost gate fails without length guidance
About 15%, which passes the cost gate with a warning
About 6%, which passes the gate comfortably
mcq.why: 0.60 × 38% ≈ 23% more per task.

mcq.q: A provider announces that a model version retires in 90 days. Three features use it, but nobody knows which. What practice was missing?
options: A larger budget for emergency migrations
Calling the “latest” alias so retirements never matter
A model inventory and a retirement calendar with owners
A contract that forbids the provider from retiring models
mcq.why: Tracking which features use which versions makes deprecations plannable.
distractors: Money does not show what to migrate.

mcq.q: Why is the diff between an AI draft and the sent version valuable?
options: It is free storage for the team's archive of replies
It gives an automatic quality metric and, after review, training data
It shows how fast each user types and edits drafts
It measures the latency of each reply the model writes
mcq.why: Edit fraction tracks quality per prompt version.

mcq.q: A draft of 200 characters has 50 characters changed before sending. What is the edit fraction?
How should new labels be split?
options: All of them into the training pool, for more data
Held-out evaluation and training pools, never mixed
Randomly reused in both pools at the same time
All of them into the evaluation pool, for coverage
mcq.why: Mixing makes evaluation measure memory.
distractors: That leaks test data into training.

mcq.q: Choose all the retraining triggers the chapter lists.
options: A team member's birthday
Quality SLO breach for N days
Drift beyond threshold
Enough new labelled data or a new base model
mcq.why: Also a policy change. Triggers open a work item; gates still apply.

mcq.q: Why re-run the full suite weekly even without changes?
options: To use spare GPU capacity at the weekends
Because test results expire after one week
It is not needed if nothing in the code changed
Providers, documents and users change underneath you
mcq.why: Scheduled re-evaluation catches silent changes.

mcq.q: How often should the evaluation set itself be refreshed?
options: Daily, from yesterday's traffic
Only after an incident
Quarterly, with new samples
Never, to keep comparisons fair
mcq.why: So it does not go stale.

mcq.q: Why not feed user corrections straight into training?
options: Training cannot use text corrections at all
They are always correct, so no check is needed
They are too few to matter for training
Some are wrong, malicious or out of scope
mcq.why: Review them first.

mcq.q: A recurring failure on a new document type appears. What comes first?
options: Fix the parser, add a case; train only if a gap remains
Ignore it, as it is probably a one-off
Retrain the whole model immediately on it
Switch to a newer model from another provider
mcq.why: Fix root causes in the cheapest place.

mcq.q: For DPO pairs from draft edits, which is “rejected”?
options: The sent version
Neither
Both
The AI draft
mcq.why: The sent version is preferred, after review.

mcq.q: What should a met retraining trigger do?
options: Retrain and deploy the new model automatically
Open a work item; retraining still passes every gate
Delete the old model at once to save storage
Nothing until the next quarterly planning cycle
mcq.why: Triggers start work, not releases.

mcq.q: Of 2,000 AI-drafted replies, 1,500 were sent with light edits, 300 were heavily edited and 200 were discarded. What share were heavily edited or discarded?
distractors: That counts only the heavy edits.
That is the lightly edited share.

mcq.q: A retraining trigger is set at 2,000 new corrected examples, and 2,300 have arrived. What should happen?
options: All 2,300 examples go into the evaluation set
The model retrains and deploys automatically tonight
Nothing until the next quarterly review
A work item opens; any retrained model still passes every gate
mcq.why: Triggers start work; they do not bypass gates.
distractors: New labels are split between evaluation and training.
Triggers exist so the team acts.

mcq.q: Who should be accountable for an AI system?
options: Everyone on the team, sharing it equally
Nobody in particular; it is shared
A named team, with an owner per component
The model provider that serves it
mcq.why: Quality, cost, incidents and compliance need owners.
distractors: Providers do not own your system.

mcq.q: A RACI chart marks the product owner “A” and AI engineering “R” for cost budgets. What does the product owner's “A” mean?
options: Assisted
Approved
Accountable
Assigned
mcq.why: R = responsible, C = consulted, I = informed.

mcq.q: Before an assistant launches, a review must confirm that it can actually be operated. Which items should the review verify? Choose all that apply.
options: A successful demo only
SLOs, dashboards and alerts live
Capacity plan from measured numbers and DR tested
Runbooks written and tested, on-call staffed
mcq.why: Plus security review and cost budgets.

mcq.q: What do release notes per manifest include?
options: Only the version number and the date of the release
Nothing beyond the release ID and who approved it
Marketing copy written for the users and customers
Changes, eval results vs before, limits, rollout and rollback
mcq.why: Readers can judge the release.

mcq.q: What makes a good service handover?
options: Walkthroughs, access, drills, shadow on-call and joint ownership
A demo of the main features for the receiving team
An email with the repository link and a short summary
An architecture diagram with the main data flows
mcq.why: The original team steps back only after joint ownership.

mcq.q: A system card describes…
options: The office layout of the owning team
The prices charged to each customer
Only the weights of the model inside it
Intended use, risks and controls of the system
mcq.why: Used for governance (16.8).

mcq.q: In the example RACI, who is accountable for threat model and data protection?
options: Platform and SRE team
Security & compliance
Product owner of it
AI engineering team
mcq.why: AI engineering is responsible; security and compliance is accountable.

mcq.q: A project team hands over a demo and a diagram and leaves. What is missing?
options: More slides for the handover meeting
A bigger, more capable model for the system
Nothing; the demo and diagram are enough
Runbooks, access, drills and joint ownership
mcq.why: Demos and diagrams are not a handover.

mcq.q: Who owns shared platforms such as the gateway and observability?
options: The model provider that hosts them
Nobody in particular; they are shared
Each product team, separately and alone
Platform owners, clear interfaces
mcq.why: Shared platforms need their own owners.

mcq.q: Before launch, the capacity plan should cite…
options: Measured numbers with conditions
Vendor peak numbers for the GPU
Last year's estimate, unchanged
Nothing yet; plan after launch
mcq.why: Readiness relies on measured capacity.

mcq.q: During an incident, index ingestion broke, and product, AI engineering and platform each assumed another team owned the index. What would have prevented the delay?
options: A named owner for each component, the index included
A faster ingestion pipeline
A larger on-call rotation across all three teams
A shared chat channel for all incidents
mcq.why: Every component needs an owner, as well as the system as a whole.
distractors: More people do not settle ownership.
A channel is not an owner.

mcq.q: At a launch review, SLOs and dashboards exist, but the runbooks have never been tested and nobody is on call yet. Is the system ready?
options: Yes, as long as the launch demo went well for leadership
No: readiness needs tested runbooks and a staffed, trained on-call
Yes, since the SLOs and dashboards are already in place
Yes, because runbooks can be tested in the weeks after launch
mcq.why: The review checks the system can be operated, not only observed.
distractors: A demo does not show it can be operated.
Someone must be able to act on alerts.
